title: Divisions of the nervous system
blurb: Sort any nerve, signal or body response into CNS or PNS, sensory or motor, somatic or autonomic, sympathetic or parasympathetic.
question: A nursing applicant is startled by a fire alarm: her heart pounds, her pupils widen and her stomach stops churning. Which division of the nervous system is producing these changes, and which branch of the peripheral nervous system does it belong to?

teach.body: Formally, the nervous system has a central nervous system (CNS), made of the brain and spinal cord, which integrates and processes information, and a peripheral nervous system (PNS), made of 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and the ganglia, which links the CNS to the rest of the body. In plain English: the CNS is the headquarters that makes decisions, and the PNS is the wiring that carries messages in and out.

teach.h: The whole map in one tree
teach.caption: Every TEAS divisions question is a walk down this tree: CNS or PNS, then in or out, then voluntary or involuntary, then which autonomic branch.

teach.body: The PNS splits by the direction a signal travels. The sensory (afferent) division carries information TO the CNS from receptors in the skin, muscles, organs and special senses. The motor (efferent) division carries commands FROM the CNS out to effectors: muscles and glands. A memory hook: Afferent Arrives, Efferent Exits. Spinal nerves are mixed, carrying both kinds of fiber.

teach.caption: Sensory neurons sit on the way in; motor neurons sit on the way out.
If the effector is skeletal muscle, the branch is somatic. Heart, gut wall, airways, blood vessels and glands belong to the ANS.
The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) carries most parasympathetic output to the thoracic and abdominal organs.

teach.h: Scenario: Keisha and the fire alarm
teach.body: Keisha is studying in the hospital library when the fire alarm sounds. Her sympathetic division takes over: heart rate and force rise, bronchioles dilate, pupils dilate, blood is diverted to skeletal muscle, glycogen is broken down to raise blood glucose, digestion slows and she starts to sweat. Her adrenal medulla adds epinephrine. It is a drill. Twenty minutes later, eating lunch, her parasympathetic division (mostly via the vagus nerve) slows her heart and restarts digestion and salivation.

teach.text: Classic reversals: the sympathetic division DILATES pupils and SLOWS digestion (not the reverse), and the parasympathetic division is rest and digest, not fight or flight. Also, the autonomic division never runs skeletal muscle: that is the somatic division's job.

items: CNS = brain + spinal cord; PNS = 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and ganglia.
Afferent (sensory) carries signals TO the CNS; efferent (motor) carries commands FROM it.
Somatic = voluntary control of skeletal muscle; autonomic = involuntary control of cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
Sympathetic (T1-L2, norepinephrine): fight or flight, dilated pupils and bronchioles, faster heart, slowed digestion.
Parasympathetic (craniosacral, vagus nerve, acetylcholine): rest and digest, slower heart, constricted pupils, active digestion.

summary: You can now place any part of the nervous system on the map: CNS or PNS, afferent or efferent, somatic or autonomic. You can also predict whether a body response comes from the sympathetic or parasympathetic division and name the outflow, nerve and transmitter behind it.

A.q: Which structures make up the central nervous system?
A.why: The CNS is the brain plus the spinal cord. Everything outside them (cranial nerves, spinal nerves and ganglia) is the PNS.

whyNot.1: Cranial nerves leave the brain but are part of the PNS.
whyNot.2: Spinal nerves are peripheral; only the cord itself is central.
whyNot.3: Ganglia are clusters of neuron cell bodies outside the CNS, so they belong to the PNS.

A.q: A neuron carries a signal from a pain receptor in the fingertip toward the spinal cord. To which division does it belong?
A.why: Signals traveling TO the CNS are carried by the afferent (sensory) division. Afferent arrives.

whyNot.0: The somatic motor division sends commands out to skeletal muscle, not signals in from receptors.
whyNot.1: The autonomic division sends involuntary commands out to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.
whyNot.2: Efferent neurons carry commands away from the CNS, the opposite direction.

A.q: Which effector is controlled by the somatic nervous system?
A.why: The somatic division gives voluntary control of skeletal muscle, such as the quadriceps of the thigh.

whyNot.0: Cardiac muscle is involuntary and is controlled by the autonomic division.
whyNot.2: Smooth muscle, including the bladder wall, is controlled by the autonomic division.
whyNot.3: Glands, including sweat glands, are autonomic effectors (sweating is a sympathetic response).

B.q: Which response is produced by sympathetic stimulation?
B.why: Fight or flight dilates the pupils to let in more light, along with dilating bronchioles and raising heart rate.

whyNot.0: Bronchiole constriction is parasympathetic; sympathetic stimulation dilates them.
whyNot.1: Sympathetic stimulation slows digestion; the parasympathetic division stimulates it.
whyNot.3: A slower heart is a parasympathetic effect; sympathetic stimulation speeds it up.

B.q: The vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) carries most of the output of which division?
B.why: The vagus nerve carries most parasympathetic (rest and digest) output to the thoracic and abdominal organs.

whyNot.0: Sympathetic output leaves the spinal cord at T1-L2, not through a cranial nerve.
whyNot.1: Somatic motor output goes to skeletal muscle; the vagus supplies the heart, lungs and gut.
whyNot.2: The question asks about output (commands sent out), which is efferent, not afferent.

B.q: Which statement about the peripheral nervous system is correct?
options: It has 12 pairs of cranial and 31 pairs of spinal nerves
It has 31 pairs of cranial and 12 pairs of spinal nerves
It includes the spinal cord and its 31 pairs of spinal nerves
It includes the brainstem and its 12 pairs of cranial nerves
B.why: The PNS is 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and the ganglia.

whyNot.1: The numbers are reversed: 12 cranial pairs and 31 spinal pairs.
whyNot.2: The spinal cord is part of the CNS, not the PNS.
whyNot.3: The brainstem is part of the brain, so it belongs to the CNS.

C.q: Before a clinical skills exam, Marcus notices his heart pounding and his palms sweating. Which other change is his body most likely making?
options: Slowing his heart and emptying bladder
C.why: Pounding heart and sweating are sympathetic. The same fight-or-flight response slows digestion and urination and dilates the pupils.

whyNot.0: More saliva and gut activity are parasympathetic (rest and digest) effects.
whyNot.1: Constricted pupils and bronchioles are parasympathetic; sympathetic stimulation dilates both.
whyNot.3: The sympathetic division speeds the heart and slows urination, so both parts are reversed.

C.q: From which region of the CNS does sympathetic outflow leave?
options: Thoracolumbar: the T1 to L2 segments
Cervical: the C1 to C8 cord segments
Lumbosacral: the L3 to S5 segments
C.why: Sympathetic neurons leave the spinal cord in the thoracic and upper lumbar segments, T1 to L2 (thoracolumbar outflow).

whyNot.1: Craniosacral outflow is the parasympathetic division.
whyNot.2: Cervical segments are not the source of sympathetic outflow; it begins at T1.
whyNot.3: Sympathetic outflow ends at L2; sacral segments carry parasympathetic outflow.

C.q: Which statement about the autonomic nervous system is correct?
options: It gives voluntary control of skeletal muscle fibers
It is a subdivision of the central nervous system
It belongs to the afferent (sensory) division of the PNS
It controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands
C.why: The ANS is the involuntary motor branch of the PNS, controlling cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.

whyNot.0: Voluntary control of skeletal muscle is the somatic division.
whyNot.1: The ANS is part of the peripheral nervous system's motor division.
whyNot.2: The ANS is part of the efferent (motor) division: it sends commands out.

reteach.title: The nervous system as a hospital
reteach.question: Think of a hospital with a command center, phone lines and two automatic building modes. Which part of the nervous system is each one?

blocks.body: The command center (CNS) makes every decision. Phone lines (PNS) run to every room. Incoming calls reporting what is happening are afferent; outgoing orders are efferent. Some orders go to staff who choose to act (somatic: skeletal muscle). Others go to the building's automatic systems: heating, lights, pumps (autonomic). Those automatic systems have an emergency mode (sympathetic: fight or flight) and a quiet overnight mode (parasympathetic: rest and digest).

blocks.h: Match the hospital to the body
head: Hospital
Nervous system
Example

blocks.text: Emergency mode shuts down nonurgent work, so digestion and urination SLOW during fight or flight, while the heart, airways and pupils open up.

explain.body: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord: it integrates and processes. The PNS is everything else in the nervous system: 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves and the ganglia.

test.q: A cluster of neuron cell bodies lying just outside the spinal cord is called a ganglion. Which part of the nervous system is it in?
options: The gray matter of the cord
The white matter of the spinal cord
test.why: Ganglia lie outside the brain and spinal cord, so they belong to the PNS.

whyNot.0: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord itself; a ganglion lies outside it.
whyNot.2: Gray matter is inside the cord, so it is CNS tissue, not a ganglion.
whyNot.3: White matter is the cord's outer layer of myelinated axons, still part of the CNS.

explain.body: Afferent (sensory) neurons bring information to the CNS. Efferent (motor) neurons carry commands from the CNS to muscles and glands. Afferent arrives, efferent exits.

test.q: Which neuron is part of the efferent division?
options: One carrying stretch signals from a muscle
One carrying touch signals from the palm
One carrying commands to a salivary gland
One carrying light signals from the retina
test.why: A command traveling out to a gland is efferent (motor) output.

whyNot.0: Stretch information travels toward the CNS, so that neuron is afferent.
whyNot.1: Touch from the palm travels to the CNS, which makes it afferent.
whyNot.3: Visual information travels into the brain, so that pathway is afferent.

explain.body: Both are motor (efferent). The somatic division voluntarily controls skeletal muscle. The autonomic division involuntarily controls cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and glands.

test.q: Which action depends on the autonomic division?
test.why: The iris muscles that narrow the pupil are smooth muscle under involuntary (autonomic) control.

whyNot.1: Kicking uses skeletal muscle under voluntary somatic control.
whyNot.2: Raising a hand is a voluntary skeletal muscle action (somatic).
whyNot.3: Writing uses skeletal muscles of the hand and forearm (somatic).

explain.body: Sympathetic (T1-L2, norepinephrine) prepares for fight or flight: faster heart, dilated pupils and bronchioles, slowed digestion. Parasympathetic (craniosacral, vagus nerve, acetylcholine) restores rest and digest.

test.why: Salivation is part of rest and digest, driven by the parasympathetic division.

whyNot.0: Bronchiole dilation is sympathetic, to move more air during fight or flight.
whyNot.2: Raising blood glucose through glycogen breakdown is a sympathetic effect.
whyNot.3: A faster heart rate is sympathetic; the vagus nerve slows the heart.
